newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal opposition chief pins hopes on local poll.
newsitem.headline: Portugal opposition chief pins hopes on local poll.

text.p: Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa stamped his authority on Portugal's main opposition Social Democratic Party (PSD) this weekend, but his future will depend on the PSD's performance in local elections in 1997, political analysts said.

Rebelo de Sousa, who has led the PSD for six months, won overwhelming support at an extraordinary three-day congress in Lisbon for his proposals for internal party reforms with some 80 percent of members' votes.
He also won a public endorsement from charismatic rival Pedro Santana Lopes after he appealed for party unity on the path to general elections due in 1999.

The centre-right party has struggled to adapt to opposition after losing general elections to the Socialist Party (PS) a year ago. The PSD under the firm leadership of Anibal Cavaco Silva had run the country for a decade.
"Marcelo won this congress, but now the pressure is on him in the run-up to next year's local elections," said TSF radio's political commentator Carlos Magno.
Publico newspaper said: "Now Rebelo de Sousa has carte blanche to run the party his way until local elections next year. If he loses those elections, he will probably want to step down.
"Despite his crushing victory yesterday, the party did not fall into his arms. It voted for him because there was no alternative."

PSD officials must have been relieved to have avoided a leadership crisis after Manuel Monteiro announced his resignation as leader of the smaller rightwing Popular Party (PP) last month. His authority was challenged by a hardline "Eurosceptic" rival, Paulo Portas.

The politician most closely watching Rebelo de Sousa is Santana Lopes, a former culture minister and former president of Lisbon Sporting soccer club, who had hinted he could break away from the party.

But he made a conciliatory speech on Saturday and political commentators said he would probably wait and see how Rebelo de Sousa fared in local elections in December 1997 before considering any bid for the leadership.

Despite Rebelo de Sousa's triumph at the congress, he faces an uphill struggle to the local elections as the PSD trails the ruling Socialist Party (PS) of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres in the opinion polls.
The PSD was preparing to appoint political spokesmen in areas such as health, education, economy and crime to respond more swiftly to government initiatives, party sources said.

Rebelo de Sousa, a fast-talking former political commentator and university professor, will turn his attention increasingly to Guterres now that he has strengthened his hold over his own party, they added.
His challenge will be to carve out a clear identity for the PSD, whose policies in key areas such as Europe are similar to those of the PS.

Rebelo de Sousa has said he would not obstruct the passage of the 1997 budget, due to be presented to parliament on October 15, as the PSD and the PS are both firmly committed to meeting convergence criteria for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

The most immediate worry for Rebelo de Sousa must be the elections in the semi-autonomous islands of the Azores and Madeira next Sunday. Opinion polls put the PS slightly ahead of the ruling PSD in the Azores. The PSD seems well-placed to retain control in Madeira.
